q: A project has a net present value of Rs 48,000 and the present value of its cash inflows is Rs 8,00,000. The sensitivity margin, that is, the percentage by which the cash inflows can fall before the net present value becomes zero, is:

options.A: 4 per cent
options.B: 5 per cent
options.C: 6 per cent
options.D: 8 per cent

q: Scenario analysis differs from ordinary sensitivity analysis in that scenario analysis:

options.A: Examines only one variable at a time, whereas sensitivity analysis examines all variables together
options.B: Ignores pessimistic outcomes and considers only the most likely case
options.C: Is confined to replacement decisions, whereas sensitivity analysis is used for new projects
options.D: Considers a few internally consistent sets of values of several variables together, such as a pessimistic, a most likely and an optimistic scenario

q: For a project, the net present value is estimated at Rs 8,00,000 in an optimistic scenario (probability 0.25), Rs 4,00,000 in the most likely scenario (probability 0.50) and minus Rs 2,00,000 in a pessimistic scenario (probability 0.25). The expected net present value of the project is:
Sensitivity analysis, by itself, suffers from the limitation that it:

options.A: Shows how sensitive the result is to a change in a variable, but gives no indication of the likelihood of that change occurring
options.B: Cannot be applied to projects appraised by the net present value method
options.C: Requires the construction of a full probability distribution of cash flows
options.D: Always assumes that all variables move together in the same direction

q: A project has a present value of cash inflows of Rs 9,50,000 against an initial outlay of Rs 8,00,000, giving a net present value of Rs 1,50,000. If the initial outlay rises by 10 per cent while the inflows remain unchanged, the revised net present value will be:

options.D: Rs 1,50,000 itself, since only inflows affect net present value

q: A decision tree is found useful in capital budgeting chiefly when:

options.A: The project has only one possible outcome in each year
options.B: The investment is a single once-for-all outlay with no later choices open to management
options.C: All cash flows of the project are certain and known in advance
options.D: The project involves a sequence of decisions over time, with later decisions depending on the outcomes of earlier stages and on chance events

q: At a chance node of a decision tree, a venture leads to a cash inflow of Rs 5,00,000 with probability 0.6 and to a cash inflow of Rs 1,00,000 with probability 0.4. The expected value of the inflow at that node is:
A project's cash inflow in a year is estimated at Rs 1,20,000 with probability 0.4 and at Rs 80,000 with probability 0.6. The expected cash inflow for the year is:

The possible net present values of a project are Rs 5,00,000 with probability 0.3, Rs 2,00,000 with probability 0.5 and minus Rs 1,00,000 with probability 0.2. The probability-weighted (expected) net present value is:
In evaluating a decision tree, the analysis proceeds by:

options.A: Starting from the first decision and moving forward, choosing at each stage the branch with the highest single payoff
options.B: Averaging the payoffs at the terminal points without using their probabilities
options.C: Ignoring the chance nodes and valuing only the decision nodes
options.D: Rolling back from the terminal points, computing expected values at chance nodes and selecting the best alternative at decision nodes, until the first decision point is reached

q: The expected net present value of a project is 20 per cent expressed as a rate of return measure with a standard deviation of 5 per cent. Its coefficient of variation is:
Where the probability distribution of a project's net present value has been worked out, the standard deviation of that distribution is used in appraisal as:

options.A: A substitute for the expected net present value in the accept-reject decision
options.B: A measure of the dispersion of the possible outcomes around the expected value, and hence of the risk of the project
options.C: The rate at which the expected cash flows should be discounted
options.D: A measure of the project's sensitivity to its selling price alone

q: In a two-stage project, the probability that the first stage succeeds is 0.8, and, given that success, the probability of a favourable outcome at the second stage is 0.5. The joint probability of the complete path of first-stage success followed by a favourable second-stage outcome is:
Capital rationing in investment appraisal refers to a situation in which:

options.A: A firm has more acceptable projects, ranked by net present value, than the funds available to it permit it to undertake
options.B: The government fixes the rate of return that a firm may earn on its capital
options.C: A project is rejected solely because its payback period exceeds a prescribed limit
options.D: Capital expenditure is spread evenly over all the years of a plan period

q: A project requires an outlay of Rs 4,00,000 and the present value of its cash inflows is Rs 5,20,000. Its profitability index (benefit-cost ratio) is:

A firm has Rs 10,00,000 available for investment. The indivisible projects before it are: A, cost Rs 6,00,000, net present value Rs 1,80,000; B, cost Rs 4,00,000, net present value Rs 1,40,000; C, cost Rs 5,00,000, net present value Rs 1,50,000; and D, cost Rs 5,00,000, net present value Rs 1,20,000. The combination that makes the best use of the available funds is:

options.A: Projects C and D, giving a total net present value of Rs 2,70,000
options.B: Projects A and B, giving a total net present value of Rs 3,20,000
options.C: Project A alone, since it has the largest individual net present value
options.D: Projects B and C, giving a total net present value of Rs 2,90,000

q: Where projects are divisible and can be taken up in part, the correct approach under capital rationing is to:

options.A: Rank the projects by their payback periods and accept them in that order
options.B: Rank the projects by their absolute net present values and accept the largest first
options.C: Rank the projects by profitability index and accept them in that order until the available funds are exhausted
options.D: Accept projects in the order in which they were proposed by the departments

q: Rationing of capital that arises because management itself fixes a ceiling on capital expenditure, for instance to keep within a planned borrowing programme, is described as:

options.A: Soft capital rationing, as distinct from hard rationing imposed by external capital-market constraints
options.B: Hard capital rationing, as distinct from soft rationing imposed by lenders
options.C: External capital rationing, since the ceiling comes from outside the operating departments
options.D: Involuntary rationing, since it does not arise from any management decision

q: A direct comparison of the net present values of two mutually exclusive machines having very different useful lives is unsatisfactory because:

options.A: Net present value cannot be computed at all for a machine with a short life
options.B: The shorter-lived machine involves no replacement, so its cash flows are incomplete
options.C: The discount rate applicable to the two machines must necessarily be different
options.D: The comparison gives no credit for the fact that the shorter-lived asset can be replaced and can go on rendering service after its own life ends

q: A project has a net present value of Rs 4,62,000 and the cumulative present value (annuity) factor for its life at the discount rate is 3.850. Its equivalent annual annuity is:

The present value of all the costs of owning and operating a machine over its life is Rs 4,80,000, and the cumulative present value factor for its life at the discount rate is 2.40. The equivalent annual cost of the machine is:
The equivalent annual cost method is the appropriate basis of comparison when:

options.A: Two mutually exclusive projects have the same life but very different initial outlays
options.B: The revenues of the competing assets differ widely and cannot be estimated
options.C: Two assets render the same service and only their costs differ, but their useful lives are unequal
options.D: A single project is to be accepted or rejected on its own merits

q: In deciding whether to replace an existing machine, the book value of the existing machine is:

options.A: A sunk cost, irrelevant to the decision; what matters is its current realisable (salvage) value
options.B: Fully relevant, and must be added to the cost of the new machine
options.C: Relevant only if the machine has not been fully depreciated
options.D: To be treated as a cash inflow of the replacement proposal

q: A new machine costs Rs 5,00,000. The old machine it would replace can be sold now for Rs 80,000. Ignoring tax, the incremental initial cash outlay of the replacement proposal is:
In a replacement study, the existing asset whose retention is being considered is conventionally called:

options.A: The challenger
options.B: The defender
options.C: The abandoned asset
options.D: The sunk asset

q: In capital budgeting, the nominal (money) rate of return is related to the real rate of return and the rate of inflation in that the nominal rate:

options.A: Is simply the real rate minus the rate of inflation
options.B: Is unaffected by inflation, which concerns cash flows alone
options.C: Embodies both the real return and compensation for the expected erosion of purchasing power, the exact relation being (1 + nominal rate) = (1 + real rate) x (1 + inflation rate)
options.D: Is always equal to the real rate plus twice the rate of inflation

q: The nominal rate of return required on an investment is 15 per cent and the expected rate of inflation is 6 per cent. The real rate of return is approximately:

options.A: 8.5 per cent
options.B: 9.0 per cent
options.C: 21.0 per cent
options.D: 15.0 per cent

q: The real rate of return required is 8 per cent and the expected rate of inflation is 5 per cent. The nominal rate to be used for discounting nominal cash flows is:

options.A: 13.0 per cent
options.B: 3.0 per cent
options.C: 8.0 per cent
options.D: 13.4 per cent

q: A project is expected to yield a nominal cash inflow of Rs 2,12,000 at the end of Year 1, when the general rate of inflation is 6 per cent. The same inflow expressed in real (Year 0 purchasing power) terms is:
Consistency in appraising a project under inflation requires that:

options.A: Nominal cash flows be discounted at the real rate, so that the project appears more attractive
options.B: Real cash flows be discounted at the nominal rate, so that the project appears less attractive
options.C: Nominal cash flows be discounted at the nominal rate, or real cash flows at the real rate; mixing the two bases distorts the net present value
options.D: Cash flows be left unadjusted for inflation, since inflation affects all projects equally

q: In a lease-versus-buy appraisal, the usual procedure is to:

options.A: Compare the undiscounted total of the lease rentals with the purchase price of the asset
options.B: Discount the cost of owning at the risk-free rate and the lease rentals at the cost of equity
options.C: Treat the lease rentals as revenue expenditure and exclude them from the appraisal altogether
options.D: Compare the present value of the after-tax cost of leasing with the present value of the after-tax cost of owning, discounting at the after-tax cost of borrowing

q: An asset can be taken on lease for an annual rental of Rs 1,10,000 payable for 5 years, the annuity present value factor for 5 years at the appropriate discount rate being 3.791. Ignoring tax, the present value of the lease rentals is:
Leasing is best viewed, for the purpose of investment appraisal, as:

options.A: A method of increasing the operating efficiency of the asset
options.B: A way of obtaining the asset without any cost to the lessee
options.C: An alternative source of finance for acquiring the use of the asset, to be compared with borrowing and buying rather than appraised as an operating decision alone
options.D: A device confined to assets that have no resale value

q: The simulation (Monte Carlo) approach to risky investment appraisal consists of:

options.A: Repeating the sensitivity analysis for each variable in turn and averaging the results
options.B: Assigning probability distributions to the key variables, repeatedly drawing values at random from them, and so building up a probability distribution of the project's net present value
options.C: Simulating the physical working of the plant before it is installed
options.D: Replacing all uncertain cash flows by their certainty equivalents

q: Where the expected net present value of a project is positive but its probability distribution shows a substantial chance of a large negative outcome, a prudent appraisal would:

options.A: Accept the project automatically, since the expected value alone governs the decision
options.B: Reject the project automatically, since any chance of loss is unacceptable
options.C: Discount the expected cash flows at the risk-free rate and accept the project
options.D: Treat the expected value as only one part of the evidence and weigh the dispersion and downside risk, the firm's capacity to bear loss and any risk-reducing measures before deciding

q: A fixed cost is directly traceable to a division and will disappear if the division is closed, but the divisional manager had no say in incurring it and cannot influence its amount during the period. In segment reporting, such a cost is correctly described as:

options.A: A controllable cost of the division, because it is traceable to it
options.B: A common cost of the enterprise as a whole
options.C: A variable cost of the division, because it disappears on closure
options.D: A direct but uncontrollable cost of the division — deducted to arrive at the segment margin, but excluded when judging the manager himself

q: A segment reports sales of Rs 18,00,000, variable costs of Rs 10,80,000 and direct fixed costs traceable to the segment of Rs 3,20,000. Its segment margin is:

A division reports revenue of Rs 25,00,000, variable costs of Rs 14,00,000, controllable fixed costs of Rs 3,50,000 and direct fixed costs beyond the manager's control of Rs 1,50,000. The controllable margin of the division is:

Head office apportions its common costs to divisions on the basis of floor area occupied, although the divisions' use of head-office services bears no relation to floor area. The most serious defect of this practice for performance reporting is that:

options.A: Floor area cannot be measured accurately in a large enterprise
options.B: Common costs should never be shown in any divisional statement
options.C: An arbitrary, non-causal allocation base distorts the reported result of each division and can make a sound division appear unprofitable and a weak one appear sound
options.D: The total of the common costs changes when the allocation base is changed

q: A division has a positive segment margin of Rs 2,40,000, but shows a loss of Rs 60,000 after Rs 3,00,000 of common head-office costs are allocated to it. If the division is closed and the common costs continue unchanged, the profit of the enterprise as a whole will:

options.A: Increase by Rs 60,000
options.B: Fall by Rs 2,40,000, because the contribution the division was making towards the common costs is lost while those costs remain
options.C: Increase by Rs 2,40,000
options.D: Remain unchanged, because only allocated costs are affected

q: In full-cost segment reporting, a division is dropped because allocated common costs make it show a loss; the common costs are then spread over the remaining divisions, making the next-weakest division show a loss in its turn. This self-reinforcing process is known as the:

options.A: Death spiral of successive closures driven by allocations rather than by real savings
options.B: Learning curve effect in segment reporting
options.C: Ratchet effect in target setting
options.D: Contribution approach to segment closure

q: Three segments have segment margins of Rs 4,00,000, Rs 3,50,000 and Rs 2,50,000, and common costs of the enterprise are Rs 9,00,000. Management drops the third segment because, after an equal allocation of common costs, it shows a loss. The result of the enterprise after the closure, the common costs remaining unchanged, will be:

options.A: A profit of Rs 1,00,000
options.B: A profit of Rs 2,50,000
options.C: Neither profit nor loss
options.D: A loss of Rs 1,50,000

q: A unit sells the whole of its output to other units of the same enterprise at prices administered by head office, and is judged on the resulting surplus. Such a unit is best described as:

options.A: A genuine profit centre whose profit measures its market success
options.B: An investment centre, because a surplus is computed for it
options.C: A pseudo (artificial) profit centre, whose reported profit depends on administered transfer prices and does not by itself prove efficiency or market viability
options.D: A revenue centre, because it records internal sales

q: Goal congruence in a system of divisional performance measurement means that:

options.A: Every division is set exactly the same target figure
options.B: The measures on which a divisional manager is judged lead him, in pursuing his division's measured result, also to act in the best interest of the enterprise as a whole
options.C: Divisional budgets are added together without any adjustment
options.D: Head office never interferes with divisional decisions

q: A divisional manager rejects a proposal that would add profit to the enterprise as a whole because it would slightly lower his own division's measured result on which his appraisal rests. This is an instance of:

options.A: Sub-optimisation — the pursuit of a divisional measure at the expense of the overall goal of the enterprise
options.B: Goal congruence working as intended
options.C: Management by exception in operation
options.D: A reciprocal allocation of service costs

q: An enterprise investigates a variance only when it exceeds both a stated percentage of the budget figure and a stated money amount. Using both limits together is preferred to using either alone mainly because:

options.A: It makes the variance report shorter to print
options.B: It removes the need to judge whether a variance is controllable
options.C: A percentage alone flags trivial sums on small budgets, while a money limit alone lets large proportional deviations on big budgets pass unnoticed
options.D: A small variance on a very large budget may be proportionally insignificant yet large in money, and a large percentage on a tiny budget may be trivial in money — the double test filters both kinds of noise

q: The budgeted overhead of a centre is Rs 8,00,000 and the actual overhead is Rs 8,52,000. The enterprise investigates variances exceeding 5 per cent of budget. Under management by exception, this variance:

options.A: Need not be investigated, because all favourable and adverse variances below 10 per cent are ignored
options.B: Must be treated as favourable, since actuals exceed the budget
options.C: Should be flagged for investigation, being adverse by Rs 52,000, that is, 6.5 per cent of the budget, which exceeds the threshold
options.D: Should be investigated only at the end of the financial year

q: A variance is small in every single month and never crosses the investigation threshold, yet it has been adverse for nine successive months. Sound exception reporting requires that it:

options.A: Continue to be ignored, since it never crosses the threshold in any one month
options.B: Be brought to notice despite its monthly size, because a persistent one-directional trend signals a systematic cause, such as a standard that has become out of date or a slowly worsening inefficiency
options.C: Be reclassified as a favourable variance for reporting purposes
options.D: Be investigated only by the statutory auditors

q: Investigating a reported variance will cost Rs 40,000. If the cause is found to be correctable, a saving of Rs 1,50,000 is expected, and the likelihood that the cause is in fact correctable is assessed at 60 per cent. On a cost-benefit view, the variance:

options.A: Should be investigated, because the expected benefit of Rs 90,000 exceeds the cost of investigation of Rs 40,000
options.B: Should not be investigated, because the saving is not certain
options.C: Should be investigated only if the variance is favourable
options.D: Should not be investigated, because the cost of investigation exceeds 5 per cent of the saving

q: The frequency of performance reports at different levels is set on the principle that:

options.A: All levels of management should receive reports at the same interval
options.B: Top management should receive reports more frequently than operating managers
options.C: Reports should be issued only when a variance happens to occur
options.D: Operating managers, who must correct deviations while work is in progress, need frequent reports at short intervals, while higher levels can act effectively on less frequent, summarised reports

q: Beyond the budget, actual and variance columns, a well-designed divisional performance report strengthens control by also providing:

options.A: A brief explanation of the significant variances, the corrective action proposed or taken, and where possible a forecast of the expected out-turn for the full period
options.B: The personal service particulars of the staff of the division
options.C: A complete list of every transaction booked in the division during the period
options.D: The performance figures of all other divisions in full detail

q: A report that estimates, before the period has ended, the variances likely to emerge and the out-turn likely to result, so that action can be taken in time to change the outcome, is an application of:

options.A: Historical reporting after the event
options.B: Statutory reporting to external users
options.C: Feedforward control, as distinct from feedback control which reports results only after they have occurred
options.D: Exception reporting confined to audited figures

q: Costs beyond a divisional manager's control are still shown in his performance report, though separately from the items on which he is judged. The main reason for showing them at all is that:

options.A: The manager must be punished for them indirectly through his overall result
options.B: The manager needs the complete picture of the costs of running his division for his own planning and decisions, even though his appraisal rests only on the controllable items
options.C: Statutory audit requires every report to contain all costs without separation
options.D: Their inclusion raises the total cost ascertained for the division's output

q: The costs of a service department, such as maintenance or personnel, are allocated to the operating divisions primarily in order to:

options.A: Increase the total costs reported by the enterprise
options.B: Enable the service department to show a profit on its work
options.C: Punish operating divisions for using central services
options.D: Charge the operating divisions with the full cost of the services they consume, so that divisional results reflect the resources used and managers are discouraged from treating central services as free and unlimited

q: Under the direct method of allocating service-department costs, the cost of each service department is spread only over the operating departments. The method's recognised limitation is that it:

options.A: Ignores the services that service departments render to one another, so the cost charged to operating departments does not reflect the full interdependence of the service departments
options.B: Requires the simultaneous solution of a set of equations
options.C: Cannot be applied where there is more than one service department
options.D: Allocates costs on the basis of benefits received by other service departments

q: A service department incurs costs of Rs 6,00,000. Its services are used as follows: Production Department 1 — 600 hours, Production Department 2 — 300 hours, and another service department — 100 hours. Using the direct method, the amount allocated to Production Department 1 is:
The step-down (step) method of service-department cost allocation differs from the direct method in that it:

options.A: Allocates service costs to operating departments without any order being fixed
options.B: Recognises services rendered by one service department to another, but only in one direction, according to the sequence in which the service departments are closed, so the result depends partly on that sequence
options.C: Never allocates any cost to another service department
options.D: Gives a theoretically exact result in every case

q: Service Department A has own costs of Rs 5,00,000, used by Production Department 1 (50 per cent), Production Department 2 (30 per cent) and Service Department B (20 per cent). Service Department B has own costs of Rs 3,00,000 and, after receiving its share from A under the step-down method, is allocated to Production Departments 1 and 2 in the ratio 3:1. The total service cost borne by Production Department 1 is:
The reciprocal method of allocating service-department costs is regarded as the most complete method because it:

options.A: Recognises fully the mutual services exchanged between service departments, normally through simultaneous equations, instead of ignoring them or recognising them in one direction only
options.B: Allocates the costs of each service department only once a year
options.C: Uses the number of employees as the base for every service department
options.D: Avoids allocating service costs to operating departments altogether

q: The cost of a central computer department is allocated to divisions in proportion to their sales revenue, although divisions differ widely in their actual use of computing. The chief objection to this allocation for control purposes is that:

options.A: Sales revenue figures are not available division-wise
options.B: Computer costs should be treated as a period cost in all cases
options.C: The base has no cause-and-effect relation with the cost being allocated, so divisions are charged for usage they did not make and have no incentive to economise on the service
options.D: The allocation increases the enterprise's total computing cost

q: Fixed common costs of Rs 6,00,000 are allocated to a product on a per-unit basis. Output falls from 30,000 units to 20,000 units, the common costs remaining unchanged. The allocated cost per unit becomes:

options.A: Rs 20 per unit
options.B: Rs 30 per unit
options.C: Rs 40 per unit
options.D: Rs 15 per unit

q: When an inter-divisional dispute arises over an allocation base or a transfer charge, the arrangement most likely to preserve both fairness and divisional autonomy is to:

options.A: Let each division apply its own preferred base in its own books
options.B: Abolish all allocations between divisions permanently
options.C: Charge the disputed amount to the division with the larger profit
options.D: Settle the bases and rules in advance with the divisions' participation, and refer unresolved disputes to a standing committee or the common superior authority whose decision binds both divisions

q: The same cost item is placed under the joint control of two managers, so that neither alone can influence it fully. For responsibility reporting, the sound treatment is to:

options.A: Recognise that accountability is diluted — either assign the item to the manager who can influence it the most, reporting it to the other for information, or report it jointly with the sharing made explicit
options.B: Charge the full amount to both managers in their appraisals without comment
options.C: Omit the item from every performance report
options.D: Divide the item equally between the two managers in all circumstances

q: The output of a discretionary cost centre, such as a training or research unit, cannot be measured in standard units. Its manager is therefore evaluated most soundly by:

options.A: Applying engineered unit-cost standards to its output
options.B: Judging it solely on whether it spent exactly the amount budgeted
options.C: A combination of adherence to the agreed budget and work programme and a periodic subjective appraisal of the quality and usefulness of the work done, rather than by a unit-cost test
options.D: Comparing its costs with the revenue earned by the sales department

q: The foreman of a machining section is judged by comparing the actual cost of the work done with the flexed standard cost for the actual output achieved. This form of evaluation is appropriate because the section is:

options.A: A discretionary cost centre whose output cannot be quantified
options.B: An engineered cost centre, in which the proper quantity of inputs for a given output can be specified in advance, so a standard-cost comparison isolates the efficiency of the section
options.C: A revenue centre with no control over its costs
options.D: An investment centre responsible for its capital assets

q: A head office finds that divisional budgets repeatedly contain built-in slack. A corrective measure that attacks the cause, rather than the symptom, is to:

options.A: Cut every divisional budget by a uniform percentage without examination
options.B: Punish every manager whose actual results differ from the budget in either direction
options.C: Abolish divisional budgets and control all spending from head office
options.D: Have budget proposals independently reviewed and challenged against workload, standards and past performance, and reward realistic forecasting, so that honesty in budgeting is not penalised

q: A divisional manager, in order to meet this year's profit target, postpones essential machine maintenance and cancels staff training, knowing the costs will fall in later years. Judged as a human and behavioural outcome of performance measurement, this is:

options.A: Sound cost control that should be encouraged
options.B: Dysfunctional behaviour — the measure is met in the short run by shifting costs and damage into the future, harming the enterprise's longer-term interests
options.C: An example of the reciprocal method of cost allocation
options.D: A favourable variance requiring no further attention

q: In an office, unspent budget balances lapse at the year end and next year's allotment is based largely on this year's spending, so managers rush to spend the balance in the last month on items of low priority. The most direct remedy for this behaviour is to:

options.A: Break the link that makes this year's spending the base for next year's allotment, and judge the budget on needs and outputs, so that saving is not penalised by a reduced future allotment
options.B: Require all balances to be spent by the end of February itself
options.C: Increase every allotment so that no manager feels scarcity
options.D: Stop informing managers of their balances during the year

q: A manager deliberately bills in the current period certain costs that properly belong to the next period in a year when results are already comfortably above target, so as to make the next period's target easier to reach. This practice is an instance of:

options.A: Feedforward control by the manager
options.B: The operation of the controllability principle
options.C: Income smoothing through the manipulation of the timing of costs and revenues, distorting the performance reported for both periods
options.D: The step-down method applied to period costs

q: A divisional appraisal based on a single year's financial result tends to induce short-termism in managers. The standard corrective in performance reporting is to:

options.A: Judge divisions only on the current month's result
options.B: Stop measuring divisional financial results altogether
options.C: Fix divisional targets for one year only and never review them
options.D: Supplement the financial result with longer-horizon and non-financial measures, such as asset condition, service quality and capability built up, so that sacrificing the future for the present is brought out rather than rewarded

q: Participative budgeting is introduced, but divisional managers possess far better information about their costs than head office and use the participation mainly to negotiate easy targets. This shows that participation:

options.A: Always eliminates budgetary slack
options.B: Is the same thing as an imposed budget
options.C: Does not by itself guarantee honest budgets — where information is asymmetric, it can itself become the channel through which slack is built in, unless proposals are independently examined
options.D: Removes the need for any performance reporting afterwards

q: Staff in a unit quietly disregard a new standard, work around it, and cease to report difficulties honestly, because the standard was fixed well beyond what experience shows to be attainable. The episode illustrates the behavioural principle that:

options.A: Standards perceived as unattainable and unfair are rejected by those judged against them, destroying both motivation and the reliability of the information flowing upwards
options.B: Tighter standards always produce proportionately better performance
options.C: Standards should be fixed by the staff themselves without management review
options.D: Performance standards should be kept secret from those who must meet them

q: Performance reports in an organisation are used mainly to identify and punish the manager responsible whenever an adverse figure appears. The predictable long-run consequence for the reporting system itself is that managers:

options.A: Report difficulties earlier and more fully
options.B: Voluntarily disclose unfavourable information in advance
options.C: Improve the accuracy of the data they supply upwards
options.D: Conceal, delay or soften unfavourable information and act defensively, so the reports on which control depends become unreliable

q: A divisional manager is appraised simultaneously on cost reduction, output volume and service quality, and finds that improving any one measure worsens another. Sound performance reporting deals with such conflicting measures by:

options.A: Dropping all measures except cost reduction
options.B: Letting the manager discover the priorities by trial and error
options.C: Making the relative priorities and acceptable trade-offs among the measures explicit, instead of holding the manager answerable for maximising all of them at once
options.D: Reporting only the measure on which the division performed best each month

q: The periodic appraisal of a railway division supplements its financial results with measures of safety, punctuality and asset failures principally because:

options.A: Financial results of a division are wholly meaningless
options.B: Financial measures alone capture only the money outcome of a period and can be improved in the short run at the expense of safety and service quality, which the non-financial measures bring into the appraisal
options.C: Non-financial measures are cheaper to compile than accounts figures
options.D: Statutory audit of the division is replaced by these measures

q: At the concept level of responsibility accounting on a zonal railway, the headquarters service functions, such as accounts and personnel, which serve all divisions without earning revenue of their own, are most appropriately viewed as:

options.A: Service and discretionary cost centres, whose costs are controlled at headquarters and allocated to divisions on bases agreed in advance, while divisions are judged on the items they themselves control
options.B: Profit centres earning a surplus from the divisions they serve
options.C: Investment centres responsible for the zonal return on capital
options.D: Revenue centres accountable for the earnings of the zone

q: A zonal headquarters works out the full cost of each division, including an allocation of zonal common costs, for general information, but appraises divisional managers only on their controllable results. This dual use of the figures is sound because:

options.A: Allocated figures and appraisal figures must always be identical
options.B: Common costs cease to exist once they are allocated
options.C: Divisions have no costs other than those they control
options.D: Full-cost information serves purposes such as costing and overall review, whereas appraisal must rest on controllability — confusing the two purposes produces unfair appraisals and distorted decisions

q: A division is charged with the cost of a facility which the zonal headquarters decided to create and whose scale the division cannot alter. Placing the accountability for that cost correctly under responsibility accounting requires that:

options.A: The divisional manager alone be held answerable, since the facility stands in his division
options.B: No one be held answerable for the cost at any level
options.C: Accountability rest at the level where the decision was taken — the cost is reported to the division for information and included in its full cost, but the headquarters level that committed the cost answers for its justification and scale
options.D: The cost be spread equally over all divisions irrespective of the decision

q: A division's performance statement shows a profit of Rs 1,85,000 after charging Rs 95,000 of head-office costs allocated to it and Rs 60,000 of depreciation on an asset acquired under a head-office decision, neither of which the divisional manager can influence. The controllable profit of the division is:
Divisional reports prepared for internal control differ in an important respect from the segment information published in external financial statements, in that internal reports:

options.A: Must use exactly the allocations prescribed for external reporting
options.B: Are prepared only once a year after audit
options.C: Cannot show any item that is not in the financial accounts
options.D: Are designed for control and decision-making, so they can separate controllable from uncontrollable items and use whatever presentation serves management's purpose, unconstrained by external reporting rules

q: A stores ledger shows the following transactions for a material: opening stock 120 units at Rs 15 per unit; purchases 180 units at Rs 18 per unit; issue of 140 units; purchases 100 units at Rs 20 per unit; issue of 110 units. Under the FIFO method, the value of the closing stock is:

The opening stock of a material is 250 units at Rs 22 per unit. A purchase of 150 units at Rs 26 per unit is then received, after which 280 units are issued to production. Under the LIFO method, the value of this issue is:

The opening stock of a material is 160 units at Rs 25 per unit. A further 240 units are purchased at Rs 30 per unit. If 250 units are then issued, the value of the issue under the weighted average price method is:

A material was purchased in three lots: 80 units at Rs 16 per unit, 120 units at Rs 20 per unit and 100 units at Rs 24 per unit. The issue price of the material under the simple average price method is:

options.A: Rs 19 per unit
options.B: Rs 20 per unit
options.C: Rs 20.27 per unit
options.D: Rs 24 per unit

q: Materials are issued under the standard price method at a standard price of Rs 45 per unit, irrespective of the prices actually paid for the lots held in stock. The value at which an issue of 600 units will be charged to production is:

options.D: Cannot be determined without knowing the prices of the lots in stock

q: The LIFO method of pricing material issues is not permitted for the valuation of inventories under:

options.A: The Income-tax Act alone
options.B: The Cost Accounting Standards alone
options.C: AS 2 / Ind AS 2 on the valuation of inventories, which require FIFO or the weighted average method
options.D: The Stores Code of the enterprise

q: The chief merit claimed for the weighted average price method of pricing issues is that it:

options.A: Always gives the highest possible value of the closing stock
options.B: Charges every issue at the latest market price ruling on the date of issue
options.C: Dispenses with any fresh calculation when a new lot is received into stock
options.D: Evens out the effect of fluctuations in purchase prices over all the issues made

q: Under the standard price method of issuing materials, the difference between the standard price at which issues are charged out and the actual price paid for purchases is dealt with by:

options.A: Adjusting the value of the closing stock of materials
options.B: Transferring it to the material price variance account
options.C: Charging it in full to the factory overheads of the period
options.D: Ignoring it, since it is only a book difference

q: Under the base stock method of pricing issues, the fixed minimum quantity of stock held as the base is treated as:

options.A: A permanent base quantity, always carried at the price of the first lot received, with the quantities held above it priced on another stated basis such as FIFO
options.B: A quantity written off to the costing profit and loss account in the year of purchase
options.C: A quantity revalued at the current market price at the end of every month
options.D: A quantity issued first whenever any material is drawn from the stores

q: Under the HIFO (Highest In, First Out) method of pricing material issues, each issue is priced at:

options.A: The lowest price among the lots held in stock
options.B: The simple average of the prices of all the lots in stock
options.C: The highest price among the lots held in stock, until that lot is exhausted
options.D: The price at which the material can currently be replaced in the market

q: A bin card kept at the bin in the stores, as distinct from the stores ledger, records for the item of stores only:

options.A: The quantities received and issued, together with their values
options.B: The quantities received, issued and remaining in balance
options.C: The rate at which each lot was purchased and issued
options.D: The quantities ordered from suppliers but not yet received

q: The stores ledger, maintained in the cost office, is kept primarily in order to record, for each item of material:

options.A: Only the physical quantities, as a check on the storekeeper
options.B: The name of the department to which each issue was made
options.C: The balance quantity alone, without any value
options.D: The quantities and the values of receipts, issues and balances, so that the value of the stock in hand can be ascertained at any time

q: At a stock verification, the balance of an item shown by its bin card differs from the balance shown for the same item in the stores ledger. Such a difference most commonly points to:

options.A: A receipt or an issue having been recorded in one of the two records but omitted, or wrongly entered, in the other
options.B: A theft of material having necessarily taken place
options.C: A change in the market price of the material
options.D: The material having become obsolete in the stores

q: Material issued to a department but found surplus there and sent back to the stores is taken back into stock on the basis of a:

options.A: Material requisition note
options.B: Goods received note
options.C: Material return note
options.D: Purchase order

q: The goods received note prepared when purchased materials arrive serves mainly to:

options.A: Authorise the payment of the supplier's bill without any further check
options.B: Record the quantity actually received and accepted after inspection, forming the basis of the entries in the stores records
options.C: Fix the price at which the material will later be issued to production
options.D: Intimate the consuming department that its requisition can now be met

q: Normal wastage of material, being the loss that is expected to occur even under efficient working conditions, is treated in cost accounts by:

options.A: Charging its cost separately to the costing profit and loss account
options.B: Ignoring it altogether, as it involves no cash outlay
options.C: Crediting its cost to the wages account of the department concerned
options.D: Spreading its cost over the good output, so that the cost of each good unit absorbs the normal loss

q: Material in the stores is destroyed by a fire, the loss being well beyond any normal allowance for that material. The cost of the material so destroyed, net of any amount recovered, is treated by:

options.A: Debiting it to the costing profit and loss account as an abnormal loss
options.B: Loading it on to the cost of the good units produced in the period
options.C: Adding it to the value of the closing stock of other materials
options.D: Carrying it forward as a deferred charge to the next period

q: Spoiled units which cannot be rectified are sold as scrap for Rs 8,000. Their accumulated cost up to the point of spoilage is Rs 35,000 and the spoilage is abnormal in nature. The net loss to be charged to the costing profit and loss account is:

A stock of material has become obsolete because the design of the product in which it was used has been changed, and it has no prospect of being used or sold at anything near its cost. The correct treatment of this stock is to:

options.A: Continue to carry it in the books at its full cost until it is physically disposed of
options.B: Write its value down to its realisable value and treat the resulting loss as an abnormal item, outside the cost of current production
options.C: Issue it to production at an inflated price so that its cost is recovered gradually
options.D: Transfer its cost to the factory overheads of the next job taken up

q: A material kept in store loses a small part of its weight through evaporation and shrinkage, the loss being within the limits regarded as normal for that material. This normal shrinkage is ordinarily dealt with by:

options.A: Charging the value of the quantity lost to the costing profit and loss account
options.B: Reducing the recorded price per unit of the remaining stock
options.C: Debiting the value of the loss to the storekeeper's account
options.D: Letting the cost of the quantity lost be borne by the remaining good quantity, whose effective cost per unit rises accordingly
